thesis.title: A storm's first lightning flash over São Paulo
thesis.lead: Lightning usually announces itself before it strikes: the electric field near the ground changes as the storm charges up, and satellites see the cloud grow. My thesis at CRAAM, Mackenzie, uses those signals with deep learning to predict the first flash and measure how much warning time each sensor contributes.
thesis.question: How much warning time does each sensor (surface electric field, satellite and detection networks) contribute to predicting a storm's first lightning flash?
thesis.demoCaption: Illustrative simulation, not real data. When the field crosses the threshold the warning is issued; the time until the strike is the lead time.

data.name: Surface electric field
data.text: Electric field mills (EFM) from CRAAM and the AFINSA network, recording how the atmosphere charges up over São Paulo.

data.name: GOES-16/19: ABI and GLM
data.text: The ABI imager tracks cloud growth and the Geostationary Lightning Mapper detects lightning light from geostationary orbit.

data.name: STARNET VLF
data.text: A very-low-frequency lightning detection network, used as the reference for when and where each flash occurs.

method.name: Baseline
method.text: A warning that uses only the surface electric field.

method.name: Time-series models
method.text: Recurrent, convolutional and transformer networks that combine electric field and satellite data.

method.name: Warning attribution
method.text: Measure hits, false alarms, calibration and how many minutes of lead time each sensor contributes.

thesis.why: Lightning puts people, power grids, airports and outdoor activities at risk. Knowing which data improve the warning helps decide where to invest in sensors and how to combine them.
thesis.note: Project in progress (2026 - 2028). This page will be updated with results.

research.title: Thesis student: air quality analysis for early warning of dust storms through climate monitoring in Ica
research.org: CIEASEST, Universidad Nacional San Luis Gonzaga · funded by the UNICA 2023 Scientific Research Contest
research.text: I built the data pipeline behind aireica.com, integrating four instrument groups: particulate matter sensors (PM2.5, PM10), an atmospheric electric field sensor as a storm precursor, weather stations (wind, temperature, humidity, pressure) and cameras that validate every alert. Python and SQL processing on self-configured Linux virtual machines, with Power BI dashboards. The platform issued a public alert during the extreme dust event of 31 July 2025.
